# 19-veles — sources

Back-test entry `19-veles.yaml`: Veles, a pricing copilot for enterprise sales teams (YC Winter 2024, W24).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's choice"
marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC post of
2024-02-23 and the months around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era where one exists;
anything later is marked as later, and a later price sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Veles - Your copilot for enterprise sales", 2024-02-23 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/KTD-veles-your-copilot-for-enterprise-sales
- [HOME24] getveles.com as archived 2024-04-19 (home page with customer quotes) — https://web.archive.org/web/20240419015813/https://www.getveles.com/
- [PRICE24] getveles.com/pricing as archived 2024-05-25, the first archived snapshot of the pricing page (the next, 2024-06-17, is identical) — https://web.archive.org/web/20240525193905/https://www.getveles.com/pricing
- [PRICE] getveles.com/pricing today, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.getveles.com/pricing
- [YCP] YC company page today, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/veles
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, wholesale and manufacturing sales representatives, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/sales/wholesale-and-manufacturing-sales-representatives.htm

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Account executives who price and quote enterprise software deals; their sales leadership.
   [LYC] "equip your sales team with an AI-powered quoting tool ... give reps a tool they will actually love, and
   leadership the actionable insights they need to move the needle." [LYC] "we're on a mission to make every rep a top
   performer." → `roles[rep]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "selling software to enterprises" (the
   post's "SaaS Pricing Calculator" and "enterprise sales deals").

2. **What (the job).** Price each enterprise deal accurately and on standard terms.
   [LYC] "Pricing enterprise sales deals is a headache. Fragmented processes and tools result in subpar terms and lost
   opportunities." [LYC] the solution ensures "accurate pricing and standard terms". → `statements.problem`,
   `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** When a buyer asks for a quote and the pricing has to be worked out and approved.
   [LYC] "Many teams resort to complex Google Sheets, Slides/PPTs, manual CRM entries, and email chains just to handle
   pricing." [LYC] the tool helps reps "navigate the quoting and negotiation process effectively". [HOME24] (a customer)
   "Veles gives us those insights while optimizing a daily activity for salespeople and saving them time."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: deal quote`. Author's choice: the window {4, WEEKS} (a weekly rhythm, the
   diversity research's reading; spec 120's WEEKS) and Frequency 2 to 4 weeks out of 4. Prevalence `p_80_100`: an
   account executive on an enterprise team quotes at least once in four weeks.

4. **Which people.** Sales teams of up to ten at US software companies selling enterprise deals.
   [PRICE24] both paid plans are "Up to 10 team members". [LYC] "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ, and BI
   platforms". → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (the team and the testimonials are US; no other
   market is named).

5. **Who pays.** The sales team's budget; the sales director chooses; finance agrees to the discount rules.
   [LYC] "Leadership lacks scalable insight into sales negotiations, hindering optimization and guidance for sales
   reps." [HOME24] the quoted customers are a "Founder & CEO", a "President & Cofounder" and a "VP of Business
   Development". → `persona.decision_maker: {role: director}`, Buyer and payer tests "The CFO" (a RevOps lead listed).
   Author's choice: no source names the buyer's title or who must agree; the CFO is the author's reading of "deal desk
   rules" and "minimize discounting" (discount policy is finance's). Purchase friction's three items (a CRM check —
   tested; agreeing the discount rules with finance; a security review) are the author's, the first from [LYC]
   "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ, and BI platforms" and [PRICE24] "Pre-built Integrations" on Growth.
   Commitment's step, "try it on one sales team's deals": [LYC] "Book a demo with us here"; the trial is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** One calculator with the price book, the deal desk rules and peer benchmarks; leadership sees every
   deal's pricing.
   [LYC] "Veles offers an easy-to-use calculator, benchmarks for comparing deals against those of peers, and clear
   guidance on deal desk rules, ensuring accurate pricing and standard terms." [LYC] "SaaS Pricing Calculator: Easily
   standardize pricing and track sales rep behavior in one intuitive platform." [LYC] "designed to enhance negotiation
   skills, minimize discounting, and land larger deals with confidence." [HOME24] "Track how sales reps are
   negotiating, discounting, offering concessions, and presenting pricing to your customers."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (the deal already in the CRM — tested; a written price
   book; one tool) and Adoption friction (every quote in the calculator, not spreadsheets — tested; record each
   concession). Relative advantage's two benefits: [HOME24] (a customer) "a well engineered pricing calculator provided
   reps to close deals faster" (shorter_time) and [LYC] "minimize discounting" (fewer_attempts, fewer rounds of
   discount); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $250 to $500 per sales team a month; the cost is deals lost or signed on worse terms.
   [PRICE24] "Startup ... $250.00 USD /month ... Up to 10 team members"; "Growth ... $500.00 USD /month ... Pre-built
   Integrations ... Up to 10 team members"; "Enterprise ... Contact Sales". → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $250 to
   $500 per sales team (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, RATE 2 to 4 deals of the deals they quote per sales team a month, lossPhrase "Deals lost or
   signed on worse terms because the pricing was worked out by hand": author's reading of [LYC] "subpar terms and lost
   opportunities"; no source gives a count or a percent. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a count of
   deals never compares with dollars). `hourly_rate` 50 (the loader wants one on a B2B entry; the chain does not read
   it): [BLS] "$104,920 in May 2025" for technical and scientific products, about $50 an hour.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [LYC] "Slow Ramp: Onboarding new sales reps takes 5 - 7 months due to poorly documented pricing strategies and
   variations across companies." [LYC] "No Knowledge Share: Top performers' insights are trapped, preventing learning
   and team-wide improvement." [HOME24] "There is also a lot of information that is lost in the front end of the
   negotiation." [YCP] (today, a later framing used only for one story) "You closed your first few deals on handshakes
   and Stripe links. Now a customer wants a ramp-up, custom terms, or annual billing — and suddenly you're duct-taping
   spreadsheets to your CRM."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Account executives (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Jordan Okafor → [LYC] "Google Sheets, Slides/PPTs, manual CRM entries, and email chains"; the ramp and the two-day approval wait are the author's.
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [LYC] the slow ramp and "poorly documented pricing strategies"; a new rep asking three people.
- Mateo Fernández → author's invention, filling a gap: a rep whose CPQ already holds the price book, so the problem is not a chorus; against on Importance.
- Aisha Bello → [LYC] "minimize discounting"; [HOME24] "information that is lost in the front end of the negotiation": a discount given without knowing what similar deals closed at.
- Connor Walsh → author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped (rather_not_say) story, GUESSED by code.
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, habitual story with no one occasion (GUESSED).
- Tobias Becker → author's invention: a gate No (on leave in the window).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → author's invention: a gate No (only renewals, quoted by another team, in the window).
- Darnell Hayes → [YCP]'s later "handshakes and Stripe links" framing: a small seller whose deals are not in a CRM, so the tested condition fails (Compatibility only with help).
- Ingrid Halvorsen → [LYC] "Top performers' insights are trapped": a top performer who trusts her own sheet (Current solution mostly works; Relative advantage negative).
- Rahul Menon → [LYC] "email chains"; the deal desk approval and three versions of one quote are the author's.
- Sofia Marchetti → [HOME24] "Track how sales reps are negotiating, discounting, offering concessions": logging every concession is more admin (Adoption friction probably not).

Sales directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Grant Whitaker, Tanya Brooks → [HOME24] the customers' praise ("gives us insights we haven't had before"): pay within the plans, the CFO agrees.
- Kwabena Asante → [PRICE24] "Enterprise ... Contact Sales": a larger team that would pay above $500 (beyond the founder's band).
- Lucia Moreno, Elena Petrova → [LYC] "Book a demo"; [LYC] "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ": would start only after a demo or a live-deal trial.
- Heather Lindqvist → author's invention: a small team that would pay under $250 until it is proven.
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention, filling a gap: a team whose CPQ already quotes; Nothing as the cost, would not pay.
- Victor Nakamura → author's invention: the price set against what the CRM costs; someone else agreed.

The share at or above $250 (5 of 8) is the author's: no public account gives Veles's conversion at launch; the
customer quotes on [HOME24] are vendor-curated. No respondent carries the name of a customer, commenter or founder.

## Status today

Widened. [YCP] now reads "CPQ for humans and agents" and addresses early-stage founders ("Veles is built for you. AI
agents handle quoting, approvals, and deal docs end-to-end so you can run a real sales motion without hiring a deal
desk."). Price today, [PRICE]: "Pay per active contract, not per seat"; "$ 8 / contract / mo First 10 contracts free.
Unlimited seats. No credit card required to start."; Enterprise "Custom". The launch-era per-team plans ($250 and $500 a
month) are gone.

## Could not be sourced

- **The cost.** The launch post names the loss ("subpar terms and lost opportunities") but no number; the 2 to 4 deals
  per sales team a month is the author's reading in the founder's terms, chosen as a count a sales director can recall.
- **The price at launch itself.** The first archived pricing page is three months after the Launch YC post; it is
  used as the launch-era price (no earlier price is public).
- **The buyer's title and who must agree.** No source names them; "Sales directors" and "The CFO" are the author's.
- **A launch-era rate of how often a rep quotes.** The weekly rhythm is the diversity research's reading; [LYC] says
  only that pricing is handled per deal.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person rep accounts.** None exists; the occasions are scripted from [LYC], [HOME24]
  (vendor-curated quotes) and one later framing from [YCP].
- The launch post's quota line ("On average 60% of sales reps hit quota due to fragmented tooling") reads as if
  "miss" was meant; it is not used as a figure.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction items, the Purchase friction items but the CRM check, and every pick are the
  author's.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Heather and Victor both say a small team needs proof it pays off (shorter quotes, bigger deals) before paying more, so the plainly named group fits, and Samuel's 'our CPQ already does this' objection is a different point that rightly stands alone.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all three speak to what would make it worth the price.

whys.g1: Both answers are about wanting to see the tool proven on our own pricing and live CRM deals before the team changes how it quotes, so one group named "Seeing it work on real data first" is exactly how I'd file them, and the name is plain.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, so nothing could have been let in.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem, idea and who pays, but 'How should directors answer?' (24) comes under INTERVIEWS · SENT, after the study has gone out, when it belongs with screen 23 before anything is sent.
founder.missing: Nothing asks about the second user my product serves: leadership, who use Veles to see how every rep is pricing and discounting. That is half my pitch and a large part of why a sales director would pay, but the flow only asks about the account executive as user and the director as payer.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It moves sensibly from the problem I have today, to what it's worth, to where the budget comes from and who approves it, then the CRM check and finally whether I'd trial it.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: What we use for pricing and approvals today (spreadsheets, a CPQ tool, or the deal desk), and how many sales teams or reps it would cover, since that drives the total cost more than the per-team price.

screens.why3: A sales director buying for a team of up to ten knows whether IT, finance and a CRM fit check stand between them and a $250 to $500 a month tool.
screens.why4: My three items are right, but 'A signed contract' is the purchase itself rather than something that has to happen first, and at $250 a month on a self-serve plan there often is none.
screens.why5: The CRM check, the discount rules with finance and the security review are what I meant, and the belief keeps the CRM check as the one tested, with a plausible two-week bar.
screens.instead: Keep the first three rows: A check that it works with our CRM / Agreeing the discount rules with finance / A security review by IT. Drop 'A signed contract'.

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, it is obvious to choose which one step to test and say how long I expect it to take.
screens.why2: The list and time box are plain, but the intro's 'how long would this step take before it went through' needs a second read, and the same hint is printed twice.
screens.why3: I know how long a CRM integration check takes for a ten-person sales team, so I can estimate it from my own deals.
screens.why4: My three steps are there in my words, but 'A signed contract' is a fourth I never named and overlaps with the normal close rather than being a real blocker.
screens.why5: The belief reads back my pick and my two weeks exactly, and nothing of Veles's name or mechanism leaks into what a director would be asked.
screens.instead: Which of these steps do you want to test? (A check that it works with our CRM / Agreeing the discount rules with finance / A security review by IT) — How long do you expect it to take, start to finish? [number] [days/weeks/months]

screens.why1: After who decides, the cost, the price and what could slow a purchase, asking what first commitment I want from the sales director is the natural last piece of 'how it sells'.
screens.why2: 'First real step' with the hint 'time, data, money or a signature' is plain to a sales founder, since it is how we talk about a next step in a deal.
screens.why3: Picking the first ask of a buyer, whether a demo, a pilot on live deals or a signed order, is exactly what I decide every day selling Veles.
screens.why4: It is a free box with my own words, and 'Leave this out of the study' is the right escape for a founder who doesn't want to test commitment.
screens.why5: The belief 'the sales director would try it on one sales team's deals now' keeps my answer, and 'now' only sharpens it without changing what I typed.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want the sales director to take, for example book a demo, or run one team's live deals through it for a month?

screens.why1: Right after I named the first step, it makes sense to show me how Keel will phrase that step to strangers and what bar it has to clear.
screens.why2: Mostly plain to me, but my buyer runs a team of up to ten, so 'one sales team's deals' reads as if they had several teams, and the trailing 'now' makes me read the sentence twice.
screens.why3: Whether a sales director would trial a quoting tool on live deals is exactly what I see on every demo call, so I can judge it from my own pipeline.
screens.why4: The screen shows a drafted sentence and a bar to accept, with no options, chips or value box to judge.
screens.why5: My step was a trial on one team's deals, but the added 'now' and the 'one sales team' framing drift a little from a director with a single team of ten who would start after a demo.
screens.instead: In most cases the sales director would try it on their team's live deals for a month.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step (try it on one sales team's deals), asking whether to put a pilot offer at the end of the study is the obvious next thing before it goes out.
screens.why2: A pilot is everyday B2B SaaS language to me, and the hint spells out exactly what respondents will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want warm leads from the study is my own call as the founder, and I can answer it instantly.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it; the two options are distinct, and no escape chip is needed for a founder's own choice.
screens.why5: The respondent line "Would you try this for real?" is generic and drops the step I typed, a trial on one sales team's deals, so a sales director saying yes isn't agreeing to the pilot I actually mean.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Respondents see: "Would you try this on one sales team's deals? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks my questions belongs right before the study goes out, after the pilot offer, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but the hint packs a lot into one block (video, typing, credits, text message), and "records the voice you pick once" and "400 credits" need a second read to see that the cost is the same whichever I pick.
screens.why3: As the founder I can judge which voice my account executives would sit through; it is my own call about my own study.
screens.why4: Two voices with 5-second previews are distinct and enough, but the typed answer says "face" while the screen only offers a voice, so it is unclear whether picking a voice also sets the face on the video.
screens.why5: It keeps my audience in my words (account executives) and leaks nothing of Veles to the respondent.
screens.instead: Who should ask account executives your questions on video? Daphne is picked for you; tap Saskia to hear her. (400 credits either way.)

screens.why1: The sales directors answer on their own link, separate from the account executives' link set on the screen before, so asking how they should answer fits right here.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but the kicker 'SENT' reads as if the interviews have already gone out, and 'Daphne Daphne' with 'Hear her' and 'Still recording' run together needs a second read.
screens.why3: I know my sales directors and how they would rather answer a short study, so I can pick this from my own knowledge.
screens.why4: Voice, read-and-tap, or let them choose covers it, the options are distinct, and each readiness note is clear.
screens.why5: My buyer was the sales director, and the bare 'directors' drops 'sales', a small drift from what I typed.
screens.instead: How should sales directors answer? AI interviewer (Daphne, on video, ready in a few minutes) / Read and tap (ready now) / Let them choose

screens.why_b1: The headline says "People disagree" and puts Price's 5 of 8 beside it, but the page's own rule is that the verdict is the worst card, and Purchase friction did not hold (3 of 8 expect the CRM check to take longer than 2 weeks), so the stated verdict and its number are not the ones that decide.
screens.why_b2: Every card shows what is counted, over how many, and where the bar sits in one line (for example "5 of 8 at $250 or more · bar 6 of 8 · 1 short"), though the Ability to pay card says its 3-and-2 split three times.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment carry my lines word for word, and the rest are my price band and loss in my terms, apart from the odd "sales directors ... the deals they quote".
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: there is no line on shortening the CRM check that failed, closing the one-short gap on price, or whether to go after bigger teams, and the only statement just says who answered the paying questions.
screens.why_b5: n=8 is visible and nothing is called strong, but leading with "People disagree" when one belief plainly did not hold softens the result, and three beliefs sitting exactly at the bar with 8 people are shown as "Holding up" without saying how thin that is.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 3 of 8 sales directors expect the CRM check to take longer than 2 weeks (bar: no more than 2), most often 2 weeks to a month, so make the CRM check fast or drop it from the trial; price is 1 short (5 of 8 at $250 or more against a bar of 6), and with 8 people every result here is thin.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "5 of 7 lose 2 or more deals per sales team a month · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 5 for and 2 against over 7 with the marker at my bar, but the unit "deals of the deals they quote per sales team a month" is garbled, and my bar line is printed twice on the chart, so I had to read it a second time to see it counts deals lost per team last month.
screens.why_b3: The card is named Existing sacrifice and quotes my belief word for word: 2 to 4 deals lost or signed on worse terms because the pricing was worked out by hand.
screens.why_b4: It tells me the pain is real and sends me to the Price card next, where the stage page already said people disagree, which is the right next question.
screens.why_b5: The count line says "a small group: a lean, not a call", but the So line's flat "The cost is there" is a little firmer than 5 of 7 landing exactly on the bar can carry.
screens.instead: Just holding: 5 of 7 sales directors lost 2 or more deals to hand-worked pricing last month, exactly at your bar of 5 and a lean from 7 people; one fewer and it would not hold. Next, see whether they would pay $250 or more on the Price card.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" sits right beside 5 of 8 at $250 or more against a bar of 6 of 8, 1 short, so I know the result and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts sales directors by the monthly price they named per sales team, over 8, and the strip marks my bar at 6 with 5 for, so all three read on first look.
screens.why_b3: "Sales directors would think Veles worth $250 to $500 per sales team a month" is my launch-era Startup-to-Growth band, in my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line says I am 1 short and sends me to the Insights tab, but the three quotes already show the pattern (a small team, a team with CPQ already, a team comparing it to its CRM cost), and the screen does not say what that means for my plans.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible, the screen says "a small group: a lean, not a call", and a 5-of-8 result short of the bar is called a split, not a hold.
screens.instead: 5 of 8 would pay $250 or more, 1 short of the bar; the 3 who would not are small teams or teams whose CPQ already quotes, so test a cheaper entry plan or show quotes getting faster before asking $250.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' sits right beside '3 of 5 from money already there · bar 4 of 5 · 1 short', so I know the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts where the money would come from over the 5 directors who named my price or more, and the bar at 4 of 5 is marked; the count line says why the other 3 were not asked.
screens.why_b3: I never checked an ability-to-pay line on the way in. Still, it is built from my own $250 to $500 per sales team a month and my sales directors, so I recognise it even though Keel worded it.
screens.why_b4: 'Expect some deals to need new sign-off. Ask which budget line on the next calls' is concrete for my demo calls, though it could have said who signs off a new line.
screens.why_b5: n=5 stays visible, the screen says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and a 3-of-5 miss is not dressed up as more than a split.
screens.instead: Say who signed off the two new lines (the CFO I expected to agree, or someone else), so I know whether a new budget line is a real blocker or just the finance step I already planned for.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding count, 6 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, so I know it held, just, and why.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the eight directors' answers to the sign-off question, 5 CFO, 1 alone, 1 several, 1 someone else, with the bar at 6 of 8, and the rule line explains why signing alone counts for me.
screens.why_b3: The title 'Buyer and payer' and the line 'The sales director decides, and the CFO has to agree' are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Plan for the CFO in most deals' is a concrete instruction for how I sell at $250 a team, with the one director who could sign alone noted.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible at 8 answered and 8 counted, the result is flagged as 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and an at-the-bar hold is not called strong.
screens.instead: Plan for the CFO in most deals; but in 2 of 8 the director isn't the one deciding (someone else, or several people), so find out who that is early.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right on top of "3 of 8 expect longer than 2 weeks · bar: no more than 2 of 8", so I see the verdict and the one-person miss that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The bands, counts and for/against marks read at once, but the headline states the bar as at most 2 of 8 against while the strip states it as 6 of 8 for, and I had to stop and check that "my 2 weeks is this band's low edge" means someone saying exactly two weeks counts against me.
screens.why_b3: The title and belief line are word for word what I checked, and the CRM check is my own wording, though the bare bar line "You said a check that it works with our CRM" adds nothing.
screens.why_b4: It tells me to plan for a 2-week-to-1-month CRM check, and the two quotes on the card (a demo with our own price book loaded, and RevOps wanting it wired into the CRM on a few live deals) show me what to prepare.
screens.why_b5: The "lean, not a call" line keeps n=8 visible, but "most often 2 weeks to 1 month" hides a 3-3 tie with "1 to under 2 weeks", and "plan for a cycle of that length" stretches what 3 of 8 said into the norm.
screens.instead: Did not hold, by one: 3 of 8 expect the CRM check to run 2 weeks to a month, 3 expect 1 to 2 weeks and 2 don't need it; with 8 people this is a lean, so budget up to a month for a live-deal CRM trial with the buyer's own price book loaded.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right above "6 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · at the bar", so the verdict and the number that decides it are side by side and agree.
screens.why_b2: Six for, one probably not and one no over 8 directors, with the marker at 6, reads at once; the bar given as both "6 of 8" and "no more than 1 in 3 against" is the same line said twice, not a puzzle.
screens.why_b3: The title and belief line are word for word what I checked: the sales director would try it on one sales team's deals now.
screens.why_b4: "Book them into it" tells me exactly what to do with the six who said yes, and it is the right move for a demo-led launch.
screens.why_b5: n of 8 stays visible, the count line says "a small group: a lean, not a call", the question is shown as hypothetical ("if it were offered today"), and holding exactly at the bar is not dressed up as strong.
screens.instead: 6 of 8 would try it on one team's deals, exactly at your bar, so one more no would tip it: book those six into a trial on a live deal this week.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict (People disagree, Did not hold) with the deciding count beside it: 5 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, 1 short, and 3 of 8 against a bar of no more than 2 of 8.
screens.why_b3: Both belief lines are the ones I checked: $250 to $500 per sales team a month, and the CRM check within about 2 weeks or not needed.
screens.why_b4: The group names point toward a move (prove payoff for small teams, run a trial on real data), but no line says what to change: a small-team plan or entry price, or a price-book-loaded demo or live-deal trial as the first step.
screens.why_b5: Every count stays visible (3 against, 2 asked here, 1 asked on Price) and no claim reaches past the eight directors who answered.
screens.why_b6: Things I did not type: small teams measure my price against what their CRM costs and want proof in deal size, an existing CPQ shuts me out, and the RevOps lead gates on seeing it wired into live deals with our own price book.

screens.why1: Showing me the idea before asking about buying it makes sense, but as the very first screen it lands cold, with nothing yet about my team or how we price deals.
screens.why2: CRM, CPQ, deal desk and standard terms are everyday words to me, but calling the product 'a benchmarked deal quote' is odd, because it's a tool, not a quote, and I'd stop to work that out.
screens.why3: My AEs build and get approval on enterprise quotes every week, so I can picture exactly where this would sit.
screens.why4: A card to read with no options.
screens.why5: The body reads true to a pricing copilot, but the opening line names it as a quote rather than a tool, and 'leadership seeing how every deal was priced' sounds like someone else's pitch about me rather than to me.
screens.why6: Heard once it's seven sentences long, and the closing three-part belief, ending in a long clause about leadership, is a mouthful to hold.
screens.instead: Imagine Veles, a pricing copilot for enterprise deals. Your account executives build each quote in one calculator tied to your CRM and CPQ, with deal desk rules and standard terms built in, and see how it compares to similar deals. The people building it believe you'd get tighter pricing, less discounting, and a clear view of how every deal was priced.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what doing pricing by hand actually cost my team last month is the obvious next question for someone who would pay for the tool.
screens.why2: "Lost or signed on worse terms" is two things in one count, and "per sales team" is odd when I run one team of reps, so I'd read it twice to see whether to add up both kinds and for whom.
screens.why3: I know roughly which deals we lost or discounted last month, but saying it was *because* the pricing was done by hand rather than the buyer, the competitor or the budget is a guess on my part.
screens.why4: The box fits, but the chips give two escapes, and "None" overlaps with just typing 0, which the spoken line itself says is the same thing.
screens.why5: "Worked out by hand" puts the blame on manual pricing before I've said whether that's even how we price, so the screen leans toward the founder's answer a little.
screens.why6: The stem says well, but "a number of deals per sales team last month, or a low and a high; none is 0" is a mouthful to hear once, and the label is read out as if it were a sentence.
screens.instead: Think of last month. How many of your team's deals did you lose, or have to discount, because the quote took too long or came out wrong? Type a number, or say I can't recall.

screens.why1: Right after the idea and the question about deals lost to hand-worked pricing, asking what it is worth to me is the obvious next step for the person who signs for sales tools.
screens.why2: It is clear, but I budget sales tools per rep per month, so 'per sales team' makes me stop and multiply across my reps before I can answer.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for my team's tools, so putting a monthly number on one is my job.
screens.why4: The bands run cleanly from under $100 to $1,000 or more with no overlap, 'I wouldn't pay for this' covers the no, and 'I can't say' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: It asks plainly what the quote tool is worth, and nothing of the founder's plan or terms comes through beyond the idea card shown on purpose.
screens.why6: The four options and the two-step follow-up are easy to hold, but 'Or say you can't say' sounds clumsy said aloud.
screens.instead: What would Veles be worth to you a month, per rep? Under $25 · $25 to under $50 · $50 to under $100 · $100 to under $200 · $200 or more · I wouldn't pay for this; escape: I can't say

screens.why1: I just gave a price, so asking where that money would come from is the obvious next question for me as the one who pays.
screens.why2: Budget line, signed off and other spending are how I talk about tool spend with the CFO, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I own my team's tool budget and know whether $250 to $500 a month fits an existing line or needs the CFO's sign-off.
screens.why4: The options are in past tense for a hypothetical ('we already had', 'There was no budget for it'), and 'no budget' is a non-answer that half-overlaps the escape, though the real sources are all there.
screens.why5: It just echoes back my own price and nothing of the founder's product or terms leaks in.
screens.why6: Four short options are easy to hold, but 'Or say you can't say' trips when heard and the past-tense options jar against 'would come from'.
screens.instead: If you went ahead at $250 to $500 a month, where would the money come from? A budget line we already have · A new line the CFO would sign off · Cut from other spending · There'd be no budget for it · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after I named where the money would come from, asking whether I can sign off on about $250 a month myself or need the CFO is the obvious next step for me as the one who pays for the team's tools.
screens.why2: Sign off, the CFO and per sales team a month are all words I use every week, so I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly where my own signing limit sits and when the CFO has to come in, so this is my real situation and not a guess.
screens.why4: The four cover it, though the No-first order and the No in front of the CFO option fight the stem's 'or would the CFO', and 'several people' can overlap with the CFO; 'I can't recall one' does not fit a what-would-happen question, where 'I can't say' would.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's per-sales-team monthly unit and the low end of the price I gave, and nothing of the product's workings or the founder's own terms leaks to me.
screens.why6: It mostly says well, but four options each opening with 'yes' or 'no' against an either-or stem is hard to hold by ear, and 'or say you can't recall one' sounds wrong for a hypothetical.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about $250 a month for your team yourself, or would someone else have to agree? Yes, I could sign off myself · The CFO would have to agree · Several people would have to agree · It would be someone else's decision · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off or the CFO would have to agree, it makes sense to ask how long the remaining step before buying would hold things up.
screens.why2: "Our CRM" makes me stop and ask whose CRM, mine or theirs, and "a check ... take before it went through" is clumsy, so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: I know roughly how long our RevOps or IT folks take to confirm a new tool plays nicely with Salesforce before we turn it on.
screens.why4: The bands are clean, don't overlap and cover the range, "It wouldn't be needed" covers a plug-and-play case, and "I can't tell" fits.
screens.why5: "Our CRM" sounds like someone else's internal note pasted in rather than a question put to me, so the wording has drifted from the buyer's point of view.
screens.why6: The two-step bands say well, but the stem's nested "a check that it works with our CRM take before it went through" is a mouthful to hear once.
screens.instead: If you bought Veles, how long would it take to check it works with your CRM? Under 1 week · 1 to under 2 weeks · 2 weeks to 1 month · 1 to 3 months · Over 3 months · It wouldn't be needed; escape: I can't tell

screens.why1: After price, budget, sign-off and the CRM check, asking whether I'd actually try it is the natural last question in the buying decision.
screens.why2: Trying a tool on a team's deals is how I'd say a pilot, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I run one team of under ten reps, so 'one sales team's deals' suggests I have several teams to choose from, and I'd hesitate over whether it means my whole team or a few reps.
screens.why4: The scale is lopsided: one full yes against 'Probably not' and 'No', with no 'Probably yes' for the director who'd want to see more first.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's ask, trying it on real enterprise deals, and nothing of the product's internals or the founder's own terms reaches me beyond the idea card.
screens.why6: It is one short question with three options I can hold, and the first option is only a little long when spoken.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you try it on your team's next few enterprise quotes, or not? Yes · Probably yes · Probably not · No
